v0.3.0 was about what you can name. This one is about what you can see without asking: fufu starts answering the question you were going to spend an operation to find out, and it starts showing you the shape of the repository instead of a list of what is in it.

**What syncing would cost**

`ff status` used to report only facts. It now reports a future: whether rebasing this branch onto what it sits on would land clean, conflict, or fast-forward — answered before you spend the operation, and cheap enough to answer on every status.

The verdict is a commit-by-commit replay rather than a single endpoint probe. That costs N in-memory merges instead of one, and it buys the two things an endpoint probe cannot give you: it matches what a real rebase will do, and it can name the commit that breaks. When it conflicts you get the subject it stopped on and how many files, which is the difference between knowing there is trouble and knowing where.

The whole replay happens inside one in-memory clone of the object database. A probe writes nothing — a repository that has never run one is byte-identical to one that has run a thousand, and the test suite asserts that by counting loose objects around a probe.

Silence is the default and it is load-bearing. An axis says nothing when syncing would not act on it, and when neither would, one dim `nothing to sync` stands for both. Never "in sync", which a reader can hear as "merged".

Where fufu cannot answer honestly it says so. Merge commits inside the range and histories deeper than `fufu.futuresDepth` (200) come back as an admitted `can't simulate` rather than a guess, because a wrong verdict costs more than an absent one.

The answer is cached under the repository's own fufu directory, keyed by the four inputs that determine it — base ref, base tip, branch tip, open tree — so it self-invalidates. There is no eviction policy and no staleness clock, and deleting the cache changes no answer, only what it costs to get one.

There is also an ambient lane. `ff hook shell install` now writes a prompt hook beside the shell alias, so your prompt can tell you the base moved without you typing anything. It is read-only by construction — no capture, no journal append — gated on a TTY, and fingerprinted on the verdict's kind alone, so a branch gaining one more cleanly-replaying commit is not news. It shares one renderer with `ff status`, because a prompt that worded a verdict differently from the command would be worse than a prompt that stayed quiet. `fufu.ambient` turns it off.

**The map**

Bare `ff` was still the manual snapshot verb. It is the map now.

The map answers a different question than the other two read verbs. `ff status` says what changed, `ff log` says what happened, and the map says where you left things — so it draws branches as a tree and treats the topology as the content, with commits there to label it.

It is a skeleton, not a budget. Only the commits carrying structure are drawn — branch tips, fork points, merges, roots — and every linear run between them contracts to a single row. jj's `~` tells you there is more; fufu's tells you how much, and a bare `~` means the walk stopped with history still below it. A run of exactly one commit is drawn rather than elided, because an elision row that saves no lines and tells you less is a bad trade.

One consequence worth knowing before you look: a repository with a single local branch has no topology to draw, so it renders as three rows however long its history is.

Branch scope is ranked and bounded — local branches by tip time, newest first, top ten, with `-n`, `0`, or `--all` to widen it — and trunk and the current branch are always present so the picture has a floor and a you-are-here. The walk itself is bounded by `fufu.mapDepth` (1000).

Branch names are what the map exists to help you find, so they are called out four ways at once: a `▸` sigil, brackets, an underline, and bold. Not one of them is a color, and that is deliberate rather than a shortage — a map row already spends magenta, blue, cyan and green, and the only palette roles left mean *trouble*, so a branch name wearing one would read as a problem. Shape survives a pipe, `NO_COLOR`, a monochrome terminal and a screen reader; color alone does not. The current branch adds green over all of it: the rest reads "you could go here", the green reads "you are here".

Capture did not go anywhere. Bare `ff` still captures first like every other verb; what retired is typing a snapshot, not taking one. `ff -m` says so rather than failing on an unexpected argument.

**Two axes, one vocabulary**

A branch answers to two things, and until now fufu described them in two different dialects — a rebase verdict against a base, beside git's ahead/behind arithmetic against an upstream that, standing on trunk, was the same ref. The same fact, twice, in two languages.

They are two axes with one vocabulary now: the **base** beneath this work (trunk, or the branch it was stacked on) and the **remote** copy of this same branch. Both are restacks — something you sit on moved, would replaying onto it be clean? — so both spend the same verdicts, the same colors, and the same words.

The same verdict means opposite things on the two axes, and the line says so. Being ahead of your base is silent, because sync never merges you into your base and unmerged work is a branch's permanent condition rather than pending work. Being ahead of your remote is `2 to push`, because those are precisely the commits sync will send.

The line says roles, not ref names. A name appears only when the role resolves to something you would not have guessed — a base that is not trunk, a remote that is not this branch's own copy — because that is exactly when the name is news. Ref syntax never appears at all: `origin/feature` is a cache of what a remote held at last fetch wearing a branch's name, and making a person reconcile that by hand is the confusion fufu exists to delete.

`ff branch list` speaks that dialect too, as of this release, and it is a listing rather than a wall of text now. Each row is the map's grammar laid out as a table — the same branch label, the same `@` for where you are standing — and what a row has to say hangs on a second indented line, so a verdict can no longer be pushed off the right edge behind a long subject. It gets color for the first time. The words come from the same renderer `ff status` uses, not a second wording kept in step by hand, and a test asserts the two are byte-identical for the same branch.

**Words you might type**

Seven verbs take a short spelling — `st`, `ci`, `sw`, `br`, `ev`, `desc`, `cfg` — and bare `ff` answers to `ff map`, since every document in the project called it the map and the word was not typeable.

The short forms are curated and closed rather than inferred from prefixes. Inference fails on stability: it would make the accepted spellings a function of the verb list, so a spelling that works today breaks the day a similar verb ships, and a spelling that stops working is worse than one that never worked.

Five git words fufu deliberately does not have now get an answer instead of a parse error. `checkout`, `diff`, `stash`, `pull`, and `rebase` each explain what replaced them and hand back a line you can actually run — `ff checkout some-branch` suggests `ff switch some-branch`, and `ff diff main..HEAD` suggests `ff git diff main..HEAD`. Typing one of these is a question, and "unrecognized subcommand" answers a different one.

None of them opens a repository or captures anything. A snapshot taken for a command that does not exist would be a row on the log for something that never ran.

**Also in this release**

`fufu.ambient`, `fufu.futuresDepth`, and `fufu.mapDepth` join the config registry, and `ff doctor` gains an ambient row beside the alias row — never a warning, because an uninstalled optional channel is information rather than a finding.
